processing: Spread, fixed, cooled, lightly rolled, then dried in a part-baked, part-pan-fired sequence; accounts differ on how much of the drying is done in the pan.
harvest_season: Spring, as with other mountain greens of Zhejiang; high-altitude gardens come in later than the lowlands.
appearance_dry: Fine, tight, glossy green strands showing down.
appearance_liquor: A bright, tender green, clear in the cup.
appearance_wet: Soft, tender green shoots of even colour.
taste_profile: High, sharp and lasting aroma with a thick, fresh and brisk body and a cool, sweet aftertaste that holds over several steeps.

brewing.notes: A glass or gaiwan both work. Downy leaf clouds the first cup slightly, which is normal. Leave the lid off between steeps so the leaf does not stew.

vintage_note: Usual for Zhejiang greens: sold as the current spring's harvest, ideally drunk within the year and kept sealed and cool. Tea sold as Tiantaishan Yunwu can come from anywhere in the Tiantai range, while Huading strictly means the main peak, so the wording on the pack matters.
description:
Huading Yunwu is the cloud-and-mist green of Tiantai in eastern Zhejiang, named for Huading, the range's main peak. It is often sold under the wider name Tiantaishan Yunwu, of which Huading has long been considered the best-known part.

The gardens sit high and foggy, with reports giving a core range anywhere from 400 to 1,100 metres and more than 200 misty days a year. Slow growth in cool air is the usual explanation for the strong aroma. The leaf goes through a mixed baking and pan-firing finish.

In the cup it is more assertive than its soft name suggests: a high, sharp fragrance, a thick and brisk body, and a cool sweetness afterwards. It holds up for several infusions. Slightly cooler water keeps the briskness from tipping into bitterness.

Buy it as a current-year spring tea and check whether it says Huading or just Tiantai. Compare it with Lushan Yunwu if you want to see how much the mountain changes a 'cloud and mist' tea.
history:
Local tradition holds that the Daoist Ge Xuan planted tea on Huading at the end of the Eastern Han, and the garden is still called after him in that story. This is a legend preserved in the Tiantai gazetteers rather than documented history; accounts differ even on the number of years, giving 1,700 or 1,800.

Firmer ground is the Tang and Song reputation of Tiantai tea and its links with Japan. The tea was registered as a Chinese geographical indication in 2010.
